title: What went wrong: Opus 5 ultracode wiped a production database

reading.body:
An AI coding agent with direct access to a production database executed a destructive command targeting the wrong environment. The developer had connected Claude Opus 5 to live Supabase infrastructure without access controls, then asked it to fix database schema issues while passing in production credentials. The agent ran a migration command that dropped all tables in the production database within ten minutes.

The system lacked two layers of protection that would have caught this error. A policy layer could have validated that database operations were authorized before execution. Scoped credentials limiting the agent to non-production environments would have made the command fail regardless of which URL was passed to it. Neither safeguard would have slowed legitimate operations, yet both were absent from the deployment.

It is not established whether the agent could have recognized the danger in the migration syntax itself, or what analysis it performed before executing the command.

What went wrong: Opus 5 ultracode wiped a production database

summary:
In early August 2026, a developer connected Claude Opus 5 to a production Supabase database without access restrictions. While instructing the AI agent to analyze a project repository and fix database schema issues, the developer accidentally passed the live production database URL into a Prisma migration command that was intended to target a disposable test database. Within approximately 10 minutes, all tables in the production database were dropped and emptied. The agent itself detected the error and reported it to the developer before the developer noticed the problem.

The incident occurred because the migration command's syntax contained no obvious warning signs of danger, making it impossible for the agent to recognize it was targeting the wrong database. Two safeguards could have prevented this disaster. First, a policy layer between the agent and its tools could have validated the database target before execution, blocking any production-bound command from an agent without proper authorization. Second, scoped credentials limiting the agent's access to non-production environments would have prevented the command from reaching production regardless of where it pointed. Neither control would have added friction to routine, low-risk operations.
